description: Whoever watches the wind will not plant; whoever looks at the clouds will not reap.
summary: Sonitree is a project that turns a map of tree heights into music, so you can hear where the forests are tall and where they’re not. The taller the trees, the louder it gets, and where there are no trees, it falls quiet. It’s an easy and fun way to show people where the world’s tall forests are. Pick a 30 or 60 second journey, choose piano, harp, guitar or marimba to go with the synth. The main melody follows the median tree height. The users can upload their own map, and then the system sonifies the image.
details:
What is this project?

Sonitree aims to convert forest-height data into sound so that people can understand and explore forest structures through audio.

The project uses data from NASA's GEDI (Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation) mission.

Instead of presenting forest measurements only through traditional graphs, maps, or numerical data, our project explores an alternative approach called sonification, translating data into meaningful audio signals. It provides an alternative way to experience vegetation information.

How does it work?

Me and my teammate Neavil agreed that GEDI Forest Height was the most suitable given our time constraint, and our limited understanding of sonification. Since we didn't have any experience with sonification, we wanted to choose something feasible, yet challenging and doable.

Processing every individual pixel as a separate musical event in the raster would be computationally expensive, so we decided to reduce the raster into a smaller grid, where each cell represents the average of valid forest-height pixels within its geographical region (one of the major challenges was trying to figure out how to process the large number of values/data points in the raster. We had to shrink down the grid/raster size through averaging, even though it compromises the accuracy. In the future version we could figure out a way to keep the tradeoff with accuracy minimal). We asked Claude to come up with a program to process the GeoTIFF file based on our methodology. The piano melody represents the median forest height, while the synthesizer (background pad) represents the average forest height across the geographical regions. For the piano, the median forest-height measurement is identified for each column. These median values are mapped to musical notes in the D-minor pentatonic scale, with taller forest measurements producing higher-pitched notes and shorter measurements producing lower-pitched notes. The synthesizer communicates the overall average forest structure and the piano highlights its tallest points. Both layers are generated directly through mathematical waveform synthesis using Python, NumPy, and SciPy, without MIDI files. Our knowledge of music. We used QGIS to visualize the dataset and produce a world-map with the vegetation height mapped into a colour band, with dark green representing the a longer/taller vegetation height and light-green representing a shorter vegetation height.

We are planning to continue working on the project and flesh out our prototype to create a webapp that incorporates other datasets/resources provided by NASA. We figure that the Godaddy offer can be used to host our webapp where students or anyone interested can check out different sonifications for different datasets/visualizations.

What tools were used?

QGIS was used for initial analysis and visualization of the dataset. The global map is taken from our visualization using QGIS. Python was the programming language used for coding. We used the assistance of Claude to come up with a script to process the GeoTIFF data, create the webapp. and generate the audio. GitHub was used for code management.

Factors considered while working on the project?

1) Data Size - We wanted the webapp to be lightweight, and didn't want the client side system to load a huge data chunk. One of our main concerns was around how a python script should process a huge dataset and generate audio without any noticeable delays. We went through the Global Vegetation Height Metrics from GEDI & ICESat2 dataset on Earthdata and understood that rh50, rh75, rh90 and rh98 files (for the corresponding dimension) most probably had to be combined to create a more accurate visualization (we used the help of the user guide to understand what 'rh' meant). However, for a 100m spatial resolution, the four files combined had a size of around 25GB which is quite impractical. With the help of the user guide, we settled that rh98 would be sufficient for our prototype, along with a 1000m spatial resolution because the data size was way less (~300MB only), though it might mean a compromise on the accuracy.

2) Musically Pleasing yet accurate sonification of data - We wanted to create a webapp where anyone can easily understand data, without having to go into the technicalities and complexities so it can be accessible to people of any age. In our initially prototype, the sonified audio was honestly very unpleasant to listen because it was a cacophony of different frequencies played together and agreed that it would be jarring for another person wanting to listen to the audio. In a subsequent version of the prototype, we decided to use MIDI so we could incorporate musical instruments. But this added an extra layer of having to process the MIDI file and convert it into a .wav file. So in our final prototype, we used an AI agent to come up with a function to apply an amplitude envelope to make the sound resemble to that of an actual instrument like piano, marimba etc.

3) Visualization of the data- We didn't want it to be just a webapp where users could only play the audio, we wanted them to see how it maps to the actual map. In our current prototype, there is a vertical line that sweeps from left to right. We wanted the map to incorporate an additional layer of highlighting the points of median height along a longitude, however we were not able to implement it on time. We figure that it would enhance understanding of the sonification.

Future Works

One of the main things we understood from our time working on this project was that there are not many platforms that where you can hear sonifications of data/image. We are hoping to experiment with other datasets like the Aerosol dataset, where each greenhouse gas can be mapped to an instrument, and the concentration can be mapped to the pitch. Creating a webapp with a feature where users can upload an image and listen to its sonification is also something we are thinking about. Another idea we had was to use a 3D model of the Blue Marble instead of a flat world-map which allows you to choose a specific geographical area, this could be more engaging for students or anyone interested.
